name: Massive Qubits Needed
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Gap Between a Demo and a Threat
lesson.summary: Credible estimates put the Million Qubit Requirement for actually breaking RSA-2048 far beyond any hardware that exists today, and understanding the physical-versus-logical qubit distinction explains why the gap is so large.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter established that breaking real world encryption with Shor's algorithm is theoretically possible but requires a quantum computer far larger and more reliable than anything that currently exists. This chapter is about just how large "far larger" actually is, because the gap is one of the most important and most consistently underreported facts in the entire quantum computing conversation. The short version, connecting to the Million Qubit Requirement discussed earlier, is that credible estimates for breaking a standard like RSA-2048 land somewhere between several hundred thousand and a few million physical qubits, depending on the error correction scheme and hardware error rates assumed. Current publicly known quantum processors have qubit counts in the hundreds to low thousands.

The reason the required number is so enormous, rather than close to the size of the encryption key itself, comes down to a distinction that trips up a lot of casual coverage: physical qubits versus logical qubits. A logical qubit is an error corrected, reliable unit of quantum information, the kind an algorithm like Shor's needs to run correctly. Because today's physical qubits are noisy and error prone, building one dependable logical qubit currently requires combining and error correcting across a large number, often estimated in the hundreds to low thousands, of physical qubits. Shor's algorithm applied to a real key needs thousands of logical qubits operating together for a sustained computation, which is why the physical qubit requirement multiplies out so far.

It is worth being concrete about this gap, while noting that exact public qubit counts change year to year and should be checked against current sources rather than taken as fixed. If a leading processor has on the order of one thousand physical qubits, and the task needs on the order of one million, organized into thousands of error corrected logical qubits sustaining a long, low error computation, that is not a gap one more product announcement closes. It is closer to the distance between a single family car and a fleet of a thousand, except the qubits also need a reliability standard not yet demonstrated at anywhere near this scale.

This is exactly the kind of concrete, falsifiable benchmark the earlier chapters on Unfalsifiable Timelines and Redefining Success argued should exist and rarely does in mainstream coverage. Instead of "quantum computers could break encryption soon," a more honest claim looks like "quantum computers currently have roughly this many physical qubits, this error rate, and no large scale error correction demonstrated, against a target several orders of magnitude beyond each of those." That version can be tracked year over year against public hardware roadmaps, rather than simply reacted to whenever a headline uses the scariest adjective.

None of this is a reason for complacency, and the next few chapters get into why serious cryptographers and government agencies are already acting today rather than waiting for the gap to close. The scale of the requirement is a reason for calibration, not dismissal. Building a million high quality, error corrected qubits is an extraordinarily hard engineering problem, but it violates no known law of physics, and steady, hard won progress on better qubits, lower error rates, and error correction has been happening for years. The honest position is that the timeline is genuinely uncertain, plausibly a decade or several decades, long enough to prepare for calmly and not so long that preparation should be ignored.
